episodes.title: The Day Boston Drowned in Molasses
episodes.hook: In nineteen nineteen, a wave of molasses killed twenty-one people in Boston.
episodes.twist: The winter cold made it deadlier: as the warm molasses met the chilly air it thickened several times over, trapping victims and slowing rescuers. Years later a court auditor ruled the tank's owner responsible.
sources: HISTORY.com, 'The Great Molasses Flood of 1919' (https://www.history.com/articles/the-great-molasses-flood-of-1919): on January 15, 1919, around 12:40 p.m., a tank on Commercial Street in the North End owned by United States Industrial Alcohol released 2.3 million gallons; a fifteen-foot wall of syrup moved at 35 mph; 21 dead and 150 injured; in April 1925 auditor Hugh W. Ogden ruled the company responsible and USIA agreed to pay $628,000.

Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Sticky Science Behind the Deadly Boston Molasses Disaster' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/why-boston-molasses-disaster-was-so-deadly-180961209/): Harvard students led by Nicole Sharp presented to the American Physical Society that the extra cold made the molasses 'easily four or more times as viscous'; 21 killed and 150 severely injured; 35 mph wave; the company reportedly changed the tank's color to brown-red to cover its leaks.

episodes.title: The Summer a City Couldn't Stop Dancing
episodes.hook: In fifteen eighteen, a woman in Strasbourg started dancing and could not stop.
episodes.twist: City leaders decided the cure was more dancing, so they found halls, hired musicians and built a stage. It only spread: reportedly as many as four hundred people were swept up.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Dancing plague of 1518' (https://www.britannica.com/event/dancing-plague-of-1518): in July 1518 Frau Troffea began dancing; within a week more than 30 others; as many as 400 people eventually affected over about two months; officials arranged guildhalls and musicians, which made the outbreak worse; John Waller's mass psychogenic illness explanation is the most widely accepted.

HISTORY.com, 'What Was the Dancing Plague of 1518?' (https://www.history.com/articles/what-was-the-dancing-plague-of-1518): Frau Troffea danced alone for nearly a week before about three dozen joined; 'a stage was constructed and professional dancers were brought in' and the town hired a band; by August reportedly as many as 400 victims.

episodes.title: The War Australia Lost to Birds
episodes.hook: In nineteen thirty-two, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight emus.
episodes.twist: The emus scattered into small groups, a gun jammed, and the officer in charge said they could face machine guns 'with the invulnerability of tanks'. The birds are widely remembered as the winners.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Emu War' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Emu-War): November to December 1932 in Western Australia (Campion district); Major G.P.W. Meredith and soldiers with two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds sent to cull about 20,000 emus; kill figures (986 reported) are disputed; the emus were regarded as the 'victors'.

National Geographic, 'The bizarre story of when Australia went to war with emus - and lost' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/australian-emu-war-history): two Lewis light machine guns; a gun jammed during an ambush; Meredith said emus 'could face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks'; 'The emus emerged victorious.'

episodes.title: London's Deadly Wave of Beer
episodes.hook: In eighteen fourteen, a tidal wave of beer tore through a London street.
episodes.twist: Eight people died, mostly women and children, and the inquest called it an act of God. The famous tale of crowds drinking from the gutters? Historians say the newspapers of the day don't support it.
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'This 1814 Beer Flood Killed Eight People' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/1814-beer-flood-killed-eight-people-180964256/): more than a hundred thousand gallons burst onto London streets in October 1814; eight died; jurors declared it an 'unavoidable act of God'; historian Martyn Cornell says rumours of beer-drinkers rushing to the scene are not supported by contemporary newspapers.

HISTORY.com, 'The London Beer Flood' (https://www.history.com/articles/london-beer-flood): October 17, 1814; a 700-pound hoop slipped off an enormous cask at the brewery; the flood 'claimed the lives of eight women and children'; the jury ruled it an 'Act of God'.

episodes.title: The Laughter That Closed Schools
episodes.hook: In nineteen sixty-two, three schoolgirls started laughing, and it would not stop spreading.
episodes.twist: No toxin was found; the official diagnosis was mass hysteria, though researchers still debate it. Reportedly hundreds, perhaps over a thousand, people were affected and several schools had to close.
sources: Psychology Today (Caroline Kamau, The Science of Mental Health blog), 'The Epidemic of 1962 - of Laughter' (https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-science-mental-health/202205/the-epidemic-1962-laughter): in 1962 three pupils at a boarding school in Kashasha, Tanganyika began laughing and could not stop; by March hundreds in a nearby village had similar episodes; it lasted months and forced 14 schools to close; the cause is still debated.

HISTORY.com, '7 Mysterious Mass Illnesses That Defied Explanation' (https://www.history.com/articles/mysterious-illnesses-mass-hysteria): the 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic affected more than 1,000 people and temporarily shut four schools; the official diagnosis was 'mass hysteria'. (Sources disagree: 4 vs 14 schools, so the script says 'several schools'.)

episodes.title: The Ship Found With No One Aboard
episodes.hook: In eighteen seventy-two, sailors found a ship drifting in the Atlantic with nobody aboard.
episodes.twist: There was no sign of a struggle and months of food and water, but the lifeboat was gone. The captain, his wife, their two-year-old daughter and the crew were never seen again.
sources: HISTORY.com, 'What Happened to the Mary Celeste?' (https://www.history.com/articles/what-happened-to-the-mary-celeste): left New York November 7, 1872; found by the Dei Gratia on December 5 about 400 miles east of the Azores with six months' worth of food and water and a missing lifeboat; remains one of the most enduring maritime mysteries.

Smithsonian Magazine, 'An Abandoned Merchant Ship Was Discovered Floating in the Atlantic in 1872. The Mystery of Its Missing Crew Was Never Solved' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/an-abandoned-merchant-ship-was-discovered-floating-in-the-atlantic-1872-the-mystery-its-missing-crew-never-solved-180985547/): spotted December 4, 1872; lifeboat missing; Captain Briggs, his wife, their 2-year-old daughter and seven crew (ten people) were never heard from again. (Sources disagree on Dec 4 vs 5 and crew size, so the script avoids both.)

episodes.title: One Word Carved on a Post: CROATOAN
episodes.hook: In fifteen ninety, a governor came back to his colony, and everyone was gone.
episodes.twist: The only clue was one word carved into a post: CROATOAN. Among the missing was Virginia Dare, the first child born to English parents in the Americas, and no one has proven what happened.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Roanoke Island' (https://www.britannica.com/place/Roanoke-Island): John White's colony landed in July 1587; Virginia Dare, born August 18, was the first child born of English parents in the New World; White returned in August 1590 to find the settlers gone, with CROATOAN carved on a tree; the fate of the Lost Colony remains unknown.

National Park Service, Fort Raleigh NHS, 'Major Theories of the Lost Colony' (https://www.nps.gov/fora/learn/historyculture/major-theories-of-the-lost-colony.htm): in 1590 White found the colony abandoned and the word Croatoan carved into a post; 'no one has definitively proven what happened to the Lost Colony'.

episodes.title: The 600-Year-Old Book No One Can Read
episodes.hook: There is a six-hundred-year-old book that nobody on Earth can read.
episodes.twist: Carbon dating puts its parchment between 1404 and 1438, so it's genuinely old, yet its alphabet and language have never been identified, and no proposed decoding has held up.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Voynich manuscript' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Voynich-manuscript): about 234 pages written in an unknown language; radiocarbon dating places it in the early 15th century; bought by Wilfrid Voynich in 1912; at Yale's Beinecke Library since 1969; 'the script remains undeciphered'.

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Here's What You Need to Know About the Mysterious Voynich Manuscript' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/6-things-know-about-mysterious-voynich-manuscript-180964847/): 2009 testing dated the parchment to 'some time between 1404 and 1438'; written in a language that has yet to be decoded.

episodes.title: 72 Seconds That Made an Astronomer Write 'Wow!'
episodes.hook: In nineteen seventy-seven, a radio telescope caught a signal so strange someone wrote 'Wow!'
episodes.twist: It lasted seventy-two seconds and was never heard again. A 2024 study blames a natural flare lighting up a hydrogen cloud, but that is still a hypothesis, not an answer.
sources: National Geographic, 'Was the Wow! signal a message from aliens?' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/wow-radio-signal-aliens-mystery): on August 15, 1977 Ohio State's Big Ear telescope recorded a 72-second blast from near Sagittarius; Jerry Ehman wrote 'Wow!' in red ink; never heard again and no definitive explanation; a 2024 magnetar/hydrogen-cloud proposal.

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Mysterious Wow! Radio Signal Might Finally Have an Explanation - and No, It's Not Aliens' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/mysterious-wow-radio-signal-might-finally-have-an-explanation-and-no-its-not-aliens-180984956/): Big Ear signal lasted at least 72 seconds; Ehman: 'Without thinking, I wrote Wow!'; the 2024 Mendez et al. explanation 'remains a hypothesis' and was not yet peer-reviewed.

episodes.title: Nine Hikers and a Tent Cut Open From Inside
episodes.hook: Nine experienced hikers fled their tent into a freezing mountain night. None came back.
episodes.twist: Rescuers found the tent apparently cut open from inside, and some hikers barely dressed. Prosecutors and a 2021 study point to a small avalanche, but even the scientists say it isn't fully solved, so it is still debated.
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Have Scientists Finally Unraveled the 60-Year Mystery Surrounding Nine Russian Hikers' Deaths?' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scientists-may-have-finally-unraveled-mystery-dyatlov-pass-incident-180976886/): nine experienced hikers led by Igor Dyatlov; tent found February 1959 with a cut suggesting escape from within; two men found barefoot in underwear; 2020 inquiry blamed avalanche and poor visibility; Gaume and Puzrin's 2021 study supports an avalanche but 'We do not claim to have solved the Dyatlov Pass mystery'; critics remain.

EPFL (Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne), 'Using science to explore a 60-year-old Russian mystery' (https://news.epfl.ch/news/using-science-to-explore-a-60-year-old-russian-m-3/): the group set out in January 1959; a small slab avalanche model published in Communications Earth & Environment on 28 January 2021 shows the theory is 'plausible'; Russia's prosecutor's office backed the avalanche theory after reopening the case in 2019; 'no one really knows what happened that night'.

episodes.title: The Crime of Handling a Salmon Suspiciously
episodes.hook: In Britain, you can break the law by handling a salmon suspiciously.
episodes.twist: It's real: the Salmon Act 1986 makes it an offence to receive or get rid of fish you should suspect were poached. It was built to choke the black market, and it was later widened beyond salmon.
sources: legislation.gov.uk, 'Salmon Act 1986, section 32' (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1986/62/section/32): section 32, originally headed 'Handling salmon in suspicious circumstances', makes it an offence in England and Wales to receive or dispose of salmon believing, or having reason to believe, it was illegally taken; amended by the Marine and Coastal Access Act 2009 to cover trout, eels, lampreys, smelt and freshwater fish.

UK Parliament Hansard, 'Salmon Act 1986: Convictions' (HL Deb 05 June 1989, written answer) (https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written-answers/1989/jun/05/salmon-act-1986-convictions): prosecutions under sections 22 and 32 combined in England and Wales since commencement: 49 prosecutions (Northumbrian 2, North West 10, South West 11, Welsh 26), 39 convictions.

episodes.title: Drunk in Charge of a Cow Is Still a Crime
episodes.hook: In England, being drunk while in charge of a cow is still an offence.
episodes.twist: A law from eighteen seventy-two covers being drunk in charge of any carriage, horse, cattle or steam engine, or of a loaded gun. Cars moved to modern road traffic law, but the Victorian wording survives.
sources: legislation.gov.uk, 'Licensing Act 1872, section 12' (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/Vict/35-36/94/section/12): offence to be drunk while in charge, on any highway or other public place, of any carriage, horse, cattle, or steam engine, or drunk when in possession of any loaded firearms; current penalty a fine up to level 1 or up to one month's imprisonment; later Road Traffic Acts displaced it for motor vehicles.

University of Bristol Law School Blog, 'Mince pies, Parliament and Peculiar Old Laws: The enduring popularity of legal myths' (https://legalresearch.blogs.bris.ac.uk/?p=1797): lists being 'drunk in charge of a steam engine' among real 19th-century laws still in force.

episodes.title: Is It Illegal to Die in Parliament?
episodes.hook: Britain voted this its most absurd law: you're not allowed to die in Parliament.
episodes.twist: Myth. There is no law against dying in Parliament; it still won a 2007 poll of absurd laws, and Britain's Law Commission gets so many questions like this it keeps a myth-busting list.
sources: The Register, 'Topless Liverpudlians confined to tropical fish stores' (7 Nov 2007) (https://www.theregister.com/2007/11/07/absurdest_laws/): a UKTV Gold survey of 4,000 people named the ban on dying in the Houses of Parliament the winner, with 27 per cent of the vote.

University of Bristol Law School Blog, 'Mince pies, Parliament and Peculiar Old Laws: The enduring popularity of legal myths' (https://legalresearch.blogs.bris.ac.uk/?p=1797): 'Nor is there a law against dying in Parliament'; the Law Commission gets so many enquiries about strange old laws that it has a page dedicated to busting legal myths.

episodes.title: Why Britain's Stranded Whales Belong to the King
episodes.hook: In Britain, a whale that washes ashore legally belongs to the King.
episodes.twist: The rule comes from a medieval statute giving the monarch 'whales and great sturgeons', and it still works today: government guidance says royal fish belong to the Crown, or in Cornwall to the Prince of Wales.
sources: legislation.gov.uk, 'Prerogativa Regis. Of the King's Prerogative (1324), chapter 13' (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/aep/Edw2cc1317/17/13): 'the King shall have ... Whales and great Sturgeons taken in the Sea or elsewhere within the Realm, except in certain Places privileged by the King'.

GOV.UK (HM Land Registry), 'Practice guide 18: franchises' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/franchises/practice-guide-18-franchises): royal fish (a whale, porpoise or sturgeon caught near the British coast or cast ashore) 'belong to the Crown or, in the Duchy of Cornwall, to the Prince of Wales', and notice is served on the Receiver of Wreck.

episodes.title: London's Ban on Shaking Your Rug
episodes.hook: In London, shaking a rug in the street breaks a law from eighteen thirty-nine.
episodes.twist: The Metropolitan Police Act bans beating or shaking carpets and rugs in the street, but makes one polite exception: doormats are fine before eight in the morning.
sources: legislation.gov.uk, 'Metropolitan Police Act 1839, section 60' (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/Vict/2-3/47/section/60): offence to beat or shake any carpet, rug or mat in a thoroughfare, except door mats beaten or shaken before eight o'clock in the morning.

The Scotsman, '10 weird and wonderful UK laws that might surprise you' (https://www.scotsman.com/news/crime/10-weird-and-wonderful-uk-laws-that-might-surprise-you-3140558?page=2): under the Metropolitan Police Act 1839 'it is illegal to shake any carpet or rug in any street', but you may beat or shake a doormat on the street before 8am.

episodes.title: The Ancient Computer Found in a Shipwreck
episodes.hook: In nineteen oh one, divers pulled a corroded bronze lump from an ancient shipwreck.
episodes.twist: Inside were at least thirty gears: a hand-cranked model of the heavens that could show the timing of eclipses. Nothing that complex appears again for over a thousand years.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Antikythera mechanism' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/Antikythera-mechanism): recovered in 1901 from a wreck near Antikythera; made about 100 BCE give or take 30 years; used to calculate and display astronomical information; fragments contain 30 gear wheels; no other geared mechanism of such complexity known from the ancient world.

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Decoding the Antikythera Mechanism, the First Computer' (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/decoding-antikythera-mechanism-first-computer-180953979/): divers retrieved the fragments from the wreck from 1900 to 1901; a back dial showed the timing of lunar and solar eclipses; nothing as sophisticated appears for more than a thousand years.

episodes.title: The Lost King Under a Car Park
episodes.hook: In twenty twelve, archaeologists dug up a car park and found a missing king.
episodes.twist: DNA from living relatives of his sister matched the bones. But the male-line DNA didn't match, a hint that somewhere in the royal family tree, a father wasn't who records said.
sources: National Geographic, 'DNA Confirms: Here Lieth Richard III, Under Yon Parking Lot' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/141202-richard-iii-genes-shakespeare-science): archaeologists peeled back a parking lot at the Greyfriars site in Leicester; mitochondrial DNA from relatives of Richard III's sister matched; 99.9994 percent probability; none of five male-line descendants shared his Y chromosome, suggesting a break in paternity.

University of Leicester, 'DNA results' (https://le.ac.uk/richard-iii/identification/genetics/dna-results): perfect whole-mitochondrial-genome match between Skeleton 1 from Greyfriars and Michael Ibsen; a different Y-chromosome type indicates a false-paternity event; the remains, excavated September 2012, were confirmed as Richard III in February 2013.

episodes.title: Shackleton's Ship, Found After 107 Years
episodes.hook: Ice crushed this ship in nineteen fifteen. In twenty twenty-two, explorers found it.
episodes.twist: Endurance was sitting upright three thousand metres down in the Weddell Sea, so well preserved that its name can still be read across the stern.
sources: Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust / Endurance22, 'Endurance is Found' (https://endurance22.org/endurance-is-found): wreck located at 3,008 metres in the Weddell Sea about four miles south of Worsley's recorded position; 'upright, well proud of the seabed, intact'; 'Endurance' arced across the stern; protected under the Antarctic Treaty.

National Geographic, 'The Endurance disappeared over a century ago. Here's how explorers found the famous ship.' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/explorers-found-lost-ship-shackleton-endurance): crushed by pack ice, sank November 21, 1915; found March 5, 2022 in the Weddell Sea (depth given as 9,869 ft in a caption, about 10,000 ft in the text); remarkable condition.

episodes.title: The Teenagers Who Found a 17,000-Year-Old Gallery
episodes.hook: In nineteen forty, four teenagers squeezed down a hole and found ancient paintings.
episodes.twist: The animals on the walls are roughly seventeen thousand years old. Crowds and lights damaged them so badly that the cave was closed in 1963, so today visitors see a replica.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lascaux' (https://www.britannica.com/place/Lascaux): discovered by four teenage boys in September 1940; radiocarbon dating of charcoal gave about 17,000 years ago (dating uncertain); visitor traffic and lighting damaged the paintings and the cave was closed in 1963; replica Lascaux II opened in 1983.

French Ministry of Culture, 'Lascaux: The discovery' (https://archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/lascaux/en/discovery): Marcel Ravidat, Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel and Simon Coencas entered the cave on 12 September 1940 via a fox's den / small vertical shaft. (The popular story of a dog named Robot is not in this source and is avoided.)

episodes.title: Farmers Dug a Well and Found an Army
episodes.hook: In nineteen seventy-four, farmers digging a well in China hit a clay head.
episodes.twist: It belonged to a buried army of life-size soldiers guarding China's first emperor. Fifty years on, nobody knows exactly how many there are, because the digging still isn't finished.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Terra-cotta army' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/terra-cotta-army): found in March 1974 when farmers drilling a well discovered a subterranean chamber; some 8,000 life-size terra-cotta soldiers; part of the tomb of the first Qin emperor, Qin Shi Huang; unearthing the whole complex expected to take years.

National Geographic, 'History of China's Terra-Cotta Warriors in Emperor Qin's Tomb' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/world-heritage/article/mausoleum-first-qin-emperor): farmers near Xi'an dug a well and found a clay head, 'the first of perhaps 7,000 unique figures'; 'No one knows for certain because excavations of the pits are still ongoing'.
